deep.reconstruction:
This page has no derivation and nothing in Gauss's hand. It is a printed table of contents, in Fraktur, from a late-18th-century German textbook of arithmetic and algebra. It continues from the previous page and ends the volume's contents. The facing page, partly visible at the right edge, is a handwritten 'Vollständige Liste von Eulers Werken'.

The printed text lists these sections:

(a) End of the series chapter.
- §149–154 continued: polygonal and pyramidal numbers, and counting cannonball piles in front of an arsenal ('Kugelhaufen vor einem Zeughause'). Modern equivalents: triangular-pyramid piles T_n = n(n+1)(n+2)/6, square-pyramid piles n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, and oblong piles.
- §155–169: geometric series; Interusurium (discounting a future payment to present value); rebate and discount calculation; a little on life annuities and 'political arithmetic'.

(b) Part 4, algebraic equations.
- §170: the parts of analysis.
- §171–176: definition and classification of equations.
- §177–179: linear equations and linear systems.
- §180–181: pure quadratics x^2 = a.
- §182–186: mixed quadratics, solved by completing the square.
- §187: Cardano's rule for x^3 + p x + q = 0.
- §188–193: general nature of higher equations and their roots, i.e. the relations between roots and coefficients.
- §194: integer roots of monic integer polynomials, which must divide the constant term.
- §195: the 'impossible' (complex) roots of a pure equation x^n = a.
- §196: transforming equations using the four operations.
- §197: removing the second term by the substitution x = y - a_1/n.
- §198–199: approximating irrational roots.
- §200: general determination of the coefficients of an 'infinite' equation set equal to zero, i.e. undetermined coefficients for power series.
- §201–203: applications of §200.
- §204: indeterminate (Diophantine) problems of the first degree.
- Supplement to §80: approximating any fraction by continued fractions, 'Zähler 1, Nenner eine Kette von Brüchen'.

The textbook itself is not identified on this page. The previous page's mention of Grauman's and Reese's chain-rule layouts and a distribution plan for a district of four villages suggests a practical North-German school text; the author is unsure.

In context, this is a printed book or leaflet with a manuscript bibliography of Euler's works bound or laid in next to it in the Gauss bundle.

results.usually_credited_to: Various (Cardano/Tartaglia 1545; Tschirnhaus/Viète for removing the second term; Euler and Lagrange for continued fractions and Diophantine methods; school textbook tradition)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a printed table of contents of someone else's elementary textbook. It contains no work by Gauss and nothing non-standard.
